questions.stem: Andy, 25, has just been diagnosed with ulcerative proctosigmoiditis and is starting mesalazine under shared care. You are finishing the GP consultation with safety-netting advice. Which instruction about when to go to the emergency department is most appropriate?
options: Go to ED today if new tender red lumps appear on your shins or forearms
Go to ED today if your stools are still loose after 3 days of starting regular mesalazine
Go to ED today if you notice any mucus or streaks of blood in your stool
Go to ED today if 6+ bloody stools a day with fever, racing heart or a swollen tummy
questions.why: Six or more bloody stools a day with systemic signs (fever, tachycardia, abdominal distension or severe pain) suggests acute severe colitis or toxic megacolon. This needs same-day admission for IV corticosteroids and surgical review.
notes: New erythema nodosum needs a same-day or early GP or specialist review, not an ED visit.
Mesalazine takes 2 to 4 weeks to work, so loose stools at 3 days are expected and should be reviewed at the planned follow-up.
He already has blood and mucus at this mild to moderate stage, so this would send him to ED every day without picking out severe disease.

questions.stem: Andy, 25, returns to his GP. Colonoscopy shows ulcerative colitis running continuously from the anal verge to 25 cm (proctosigmoiditis). He has 4 to 5 bloody stools a day. Temp 36.8 °C, HR 82, Hb 124 g/L, ESR 28 mm/h. Stool pathogens are negative. What is the best first-line treatment?
options: Oral prednisolone 40 mg each morning, then weaned gradually over 8 weeks
Mesalazine 1 g suppository at night, used alone
Rectal mesalazine enema or foam at night plus oral mesalazine daily
Hospital admission for IV hydrocortisone 100 mg 6-hourly
questions.why: Mild to moderate distal UC is treated first with a rectal 5-ASA plus oral mesalazine, and the combination works better than either alone. An enema or foam is needed to reach the sigmoid. A corticosteroid is added only if there is no response.
notes: Steroids are second line, added if there is no response to mesalazine. They are not the first choice in mild to moderate disease because of their adverse effects.
A suppository only reaches the rectum (about 15 cm), but his disease extends to 25 cm, and rectal therapy alone is less effective than combining it with oral mesalazine.
He doesn't meet the criteria for acute severe UC (6 or more bloody stools a day plus fever, HR above 90, Hb below 105 or ESR above 30), so he can be managed as an outpatient.

questions.stem: Andy, 25, has 2 months of bloody, mucousy diarrhoea. His stool tests for pathogens are negative, and his faecal calprotectin is 720 µg/g (normal below 50). Colonoscopy later confirms ulcerative colitis. What is the main source of the raised faecal calprotectin?
options: Neutrophils migrating into the inflamed mucosa and shedding into the lumen
Haemoglobin from mucosal bleeding into the lumen, broken down by colonic bacteria
Increased turnover and shedding of normal colonic epithelial cells
Plasma proteins leaking across the damaged mucosa into the lumen
questions.why: Calprotectin is a calcium- and zinc-binding protein found mainly in the cytosol of neutrophils. When neutrophils infiltrate inflamed bowel mucosa and pass into the lumen, faecal levels rise, so it is a marker of mucosal inflammation that separates IBD from functional disorders such as IBS.
notes: Calprotectin is not a breakdown product of haemoglobin. Blood in the stool is detected by faecal occult blood or immunochemical (FIT) tests, which measure something different.
Epithelial cells are not the main source. Calprotectin comes mainly from neutrophils, so it rises with inflammatory cell infiltration, not with cell turnover.
Calprotectin is not a plasma protein lost through a leaky mucosa. It is released locally by neutrophils within the gut wall and lumen.

questions.stem: Andy's colonoscopy report describes continuous inflammation from the anal verge to 25 cm, crossing the rectosigmoid junction. On a teaching ward round, you are asked about the gross anatomy of this region. Which anatomical feature marks where the sigmoid colon ends and the rectum begins?
options: Dentate line, where rectal columnar epithelium meets squamous epithelium
Peritoneal reflection forming the rectovesical pouch
Puborectalis sling forming the anorectal angle
Taeniae coli spreading out into a continuous longitudinal muscle coat
questions.why: At the rectosigmoid junction (about S3, where the sigmoid mesocolon ends), the three taeniae coli spread out to form a continuous outer longitudinal muscle layer. The rectum therefore has no taeniae, haustra, appendices epiploicae or mesentery.
notes: The dentate line lies in the anal canal and marks the junction of endoderm and ectoderm. It is well below the start of the rectum.
The peritoneal reflection lies at the junction of the middle and lower thirds of the rectum, not where the rectum begins.
Puborectalis forms the anorectal junction at the lower end of the rectum, not the upper end where it meets the sigmoid colon.
